extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers studying peer review and academic publishing (especially in Earth and space sciences), AGU staff and policy makers
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing gender and age bias in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of gender and age differences in publishing and peer-review activities using membership and editorial databases (author roles, reviewer suggestions, invitations, and reviewer acceptance) to identify under‑utilization of women. Focus is on Earth and space science journals (AGU) over 2012–2016.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-reported gender and account for age
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender should be determined from self-reported data rather than inferred from first names; analyses must account for age because the proportion of women researchers decreases with age and age-stratification can reveal otherwise hidden gender differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect self-reported gender from membership databases when possible. Stratify all gender comparisons by age cohorts to avoid confounding (the paper used age cohorts across 2012–2016). Note that failing to account for age can mask or distort gender patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate by author gender (stratified by age)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare manuscript acceptance rates for female versus male first authors across age cohorts (example finding: female first authors had higher acceptance rates than men across all age cohorts: 61% vs 58%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute acceptance rates by gender within age cohorts and test differences (chi-square tests reported; include n and χ² values). Report overall and cohort-level percentages to show consistent patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of women among first authors, all authors, and membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the proportion of women in different roles (first authors, all authors, and organizational membership) as baseline expectations for reviewer utilization (example: women = 27% of first authors, 24% of all authors, 30% of AGU membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these baseline proportions to set expected rates for reviewer selection; compare observed reviewer gender proportions to these baselines to assess under- or over-utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of female reviewers versus expected (utilization metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether women are utilized as peer reviewers at rates consistent with expected baselines (finding: women were 21% of reviewers, lower than expected based on first authors/all authors/membership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed reviewer gender proportions to expected proportions derived from first-author, all-author, and membership distributions; use statistical tests (chi-square) and report sample sizes and p-values to quantify gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal trend analysis of reviewer gender representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Track changes in the proportion of female reviewers over time to see whether gaps are narrowing or persisting (finding: proportion increased from 2012 to 2016 but the gap persisted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze year-by-year proportions and present trend lines or tables. Even with increases, evaluate whether representation reaches expected baselines within age cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-suggested reviewer gender composition (by author gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the gender composition of reviewers suggested by authors and how it varies by the suggesting author's gender (finding: male authors suggested 16% female reviewers; female authors suggested 22%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate suggested-reviewer data by author gender; compare suggested proportions to expected baselines and test for statistically significant differences. Consider how suggestion patterns may propagate gender skew into invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor invitation patterns by editor gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether editor gender affects invitations to reviewers (finding: male editors invited 18% female reviewers, female editors invited 22%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratify invitation rates by editor gender, compare to suggested-reviewer pools and baseline population, and test differences. Use this to identify whether editorial assignment practices perpetuate or mitigate gender imbalances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coauthor network gender composition and its influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate coauthor networks to see whether first authors' collaborators are gender-skewed, which may influence reviewer suggestions (finding: male first authors tend to have male collaborators ~16%; female first authors had collaborators closer to population distribution ~22%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map coauthor networks and compute collaborator gender proportions for first authors by gender. Use these network patterns to interpret suggested-reviewer biases and to identify structural causes of reviewer under‑utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical testing and reporting (chi-square and sample sizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use formal statistical tests (chi-square) with explicit n, χ², and P values when comparing proportions (examples provided throughout the results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always report test statistics, sample sizes, and P-values for proportion comparisons. Provide tables showing counts and percentages for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple baselines to assess expected reviewer proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether a gender group is under‑utilized as reviewers, compare observed reviewer rates against multiple baselines (first authorship rates, all authorship rates, and membership demographics) to provide a robust expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report comparisons against all relevant baselines rather than a single denominator, since different baselines can yield different interpretations; explicitly state which baseline is being used in each comparison.
